title: Mini Decompiler
tagline: A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an object you compiled into structured C, then proves the output.
summary: A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an ELF relocatable object you compiled into structured C. It recompiles its own output, runs a differential test over an input grid, compares relocation-masked bytes and writes an evidence report that lists every unknown.
youWillBuild: A decompiler that turns the functions of an x86-64 relocatable object you compiled into one C file, and an evidence report that says what was proved and what stays unknown.
skills: Read ELF64 sections, symbols and RELA records
Decode an x86-64 subset and check it against a disassembler listing
Recover blocks, jump tables, dominators and loops
Lift to an IR with explicit flags and build minimal SSA
Fold copies, dead code and division by a constant
Recover System V parameters, pointer and struct types and signedness
Structure a graph into C without goto
Prove the output with recompilation, a differential grid and masked bytes

prerequisites.title: Python 3.10+ with the standard library only. clang is optional and enables the recompile and differential legs of stage 8.
Lessons on ELF anatomy, disassembly and control flow, lifting to pseudocode, calling conventions, compiler idioms and rebuild-and-prove.

stages.title: Read an ELF relocatable object
stages.summary: Validate the ELF64 header, read section headers, the symbol table and every RELA record, and cut each function out of .text with its relocations and its alignment padding. A PC-relative record points at S + A + (end of instruction - P), so a target is resolved only with the end of the instruction that holds the field.
stages.doc:
Stage 1 of 8. Read the [project prerequisites](https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch/blob/9712e323fde8cb2ec933310ac619e920e8e31017/projects/mini-decompiler/README.md) first. This stage applies [Program Anatomy: An ELF Reader From Scratch](/learn/32-program-anatomy-elf-from-scratch) and the relocation part of [Disassembly and Control Flow](/learn/33-disassembly-and-control-flow).

## What you build

You build the loader that every later stage reads from. It accepts the bytes of one ELF64 little-endian x86-64 relocatable object (`ET_REL`), and it gives back:

- the section headers, each with its name and its bytes,
- the symbol table, with name, value, size, type, binding and section name,
- every RELA record, grouped by the section it patches and sorted by offset,
- one function at a time: its bytes, the relocations inside it, and the alignment padding after it.

It also resolves a relocation to the place it points at after linking.

## Why it matters

A relocatable object is the output of `clang -c`. The link editor has not run yet, so every address that refers to another section is a field of zero bytes plus a RELA record. The jump table of `band`, the lookup table at `-O1`, and every call to another function are visible only through those records. If the loader drops them, stage 3 cannot find the jump table, stage 7 cannot name the lookup table, and stage 8 compares bytes that the link editor will overwrite.

A function symbol gives the start and the size. The bytes between the end of one function and the start of the next are alignment padding. Stage 3 decodes the padding with a linear sweep to show where the sweep and the recursive descent disagree, so the loader reports it separately.

## Work through one concrete case

Build the fixture yourself, or use the committed objects. The objects were built with:

```bash
clang -target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -O1 -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -c samples.c -o samples-x86_64-O1.o
```

The header of `samples-x86_64-O1.o` starts with `7f 45 4c 46 02 01`: the magic, `ELFCLASS64` (2) and little-endian (1). At offset 16, `e_type` is 1 (`ET_REL`) and `e_machine` is 62 (`EM_X86_64`). The section header table is at `e_shoff`, each entry is 64 bytes, and the first five section names are the empty null section, `.strtab`, `.text`, `.rela.text` and `.rodata`. `.text` is 0xb2 bytes long.

The five function symbols, in address order, with their sizes:

| name | value | size | next start | padding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tenths_and_fifths` | 0x0 | 0x23 | 0x30 | 13 |
| `thirds` | 0x30 | 0x1a | 0x50 | 6 |
| `band` | 0x50 | 0x17 | 0x70 | 9 |
| `fold` | 0x70 | 0x26 | 0xa0 | 10 |
| `record` | 0xa0 | 0x12 | 0xb2 | 0 |

`band` holds one relocation. The record in `.rela.text` has `r_offset` 0x5f, type 2 (`R_X86_64_PC32`), the `.rodata` section symbol, and addend -4. Inside the function the offset is 0x5f - 0x50 = 0xf.

The field belongs to `leaq (%rip), %rcx`, which starts at 0x5c and ends at 0x63. The psABI says the link editor stores S + A - P in a PC-relative field, where S is the symbol value, A is the addend and P is the field address. The processor adds the field to the address of the next instruction. So the operand reaches:

```text
S + A - P + end = 0 + (-4) - 0x5f + 0x63 = 0
```

The table starts at `.rodata+0x0`. Its first eight bytes are `05 00 00 00 08 00 00 00`: the values 5 and 8 of the `switch` in `band`.

At `-O0`, `.rodata` itself has six relocations, one per jump table entry. Each is a PC-relative record against `.text` whose target, resolved with the table base as the end, is 0x78, 0x81, 0x8a, 0x93, 0x9c and 0xa5. These are the six case blocks of `band`.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-1
```

Change the addend, the field offset and the instruction length in the lab. The target moves by the same amount as the distance from the field to the end of the instruction, which is why `relocation_target` refuses a PC-relative record without that end.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `elf` module. The starter keeps the dataclasses, the constants, `_cstring`, `_slice`, `section`, `has_section`, `functions`, `relocation_at` and `symbolize`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `ElfObject(data: bytes)` | Raise `ElfError` unless the data has the ELF magic, `ELFCLASS64`, little-endian encoding, `EM_X86_64`, `ET_REL` and `e_shentsize` 64. Read every section header; `SHT_NOBITS` has no bytes. Name sections from `e_shstrndx`. Then set `self.symbols` and `self.relocations`. Any table outside the file raises `ElfError`. |
| `ElfObject._read_symbols() -> list[Symbol]` | Every 24-byte `Elf64_Sym` of every `SHT_SYMTAB`, named through the string table at `sh_link`. Type is `st_info & 0xf`, binding is `st_info >> 4`. |
| `ElfObject._read_relocations() -> dict[str, list[Relocation]]` | Every 24-byte `Elf64_Rela` of every `SHT_RELA`, keyed by the name of section `sh_info`, sorted by offset. A symbol index past the table raises `ElfError`. |
| `ElfObject.function_extent(name, section=".text") -> (start, end, padding_end)` | From the function symbol: `start` is the value, `end` is `start + size`, `padding_end` is the next function start or the section size. Unknown names raise `ElfError`. |
| `ElfObject.function(name, section=".text") -> FunctionBytes` | The bytes in `[start, end)` and the relocations inside that range, with offsets relative to `start`. |
| `relocation_target(relocation, field_end=None) -> Target` | Absolute: `S + A`. PC-relative (`R_X86_64_PC32`, `R_X86_64_PLT32`): `S + A + (field_end - P)`. A PC-relative record with no `field_end` raises `ValueError`. A section symbol has S = 0. |

The CLI is supplied. After this stage the loader runs, and the `disasm` command starts to work after stage 2.

## Verify and inspect

From the repository root, initialize a workspace once:

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --init learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 1 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
```

A fresh workspace fails with `not implemented yet: Stage 1: implement ElfObject.__init__`. The tests check the section order, the symbol table above, the `band` relocation, the jump table targets at `-O0`, the held-out object, and these failure cases.

## Failure cases

- Bytes that start with `MZ`, or only the four magic bytes, raise `ElfError`.
- A 32-bit class, big-endian data, another machine or an executable (`ET_EXEC`) raises `ElfError` with the field that failed.
- A file cut at 200 bytes, or an `e_shoff` past the end, raises `ElfError` instead of reading garbage.
- A RELA record that names symbol 0xffff, past the end of the symbol table, raises `ElfError`.
- `relocation_at(".text", 0x60)` returns `None`, because 0x60 is inside the field but is not its start.

## Extensions

- Read `.symtab` entries with `SHN_COMMON` and `SHN_ABS` and report them as unknown sections.
- Accept `R_X86_64_GOTPCREL` and record that the target is a GOT slot, which only exists after linking.
- Read an `ET_DYN` shared object through its program headers and its dynamic symbol table.

stages.title: Decode the x86-64 subset
stages.summary: Decode legacy prefixes, REX, one and two byte opcodes, ModRM, SIB, displacements and immediates for the instructions the fixtures use. Record where the displacement and immediate fields sit so relocations can be matched to operands. Every instruction must agree with the captured disassembler listing by address, bytes and AT&T text.
stages.doc:
Stage 2 of 8. This stage applies [Disassembly and Control Flow](/learn/33-disassembly-and-control-flow), sections "The Instruction Format Has One Rule Per Field" and "Linear Sweep".

## What you build

You build a decoder for the part of x86-64 that clang emits for the fixtures at `-O0` and `-O1`. `decode(code, address)` reads one instruction and returns an `Instruction` with its bytes, a normalized operation, its operands, its operand width, its control-flow kind and its branch target. It also records where the displacement field and the immediate field sit inside the instruction. `linear_sweep` decodes a byte range in address order and lists every byte that it cannot decode.

The decoder is checked against a disassembler listing. For every instruction of the four committed objects, your address, your bytes and your AT&T text must equal the captured listing.

## Why it matters

Every later stage trusts the decoder. A wrong operand width changes a 32-bit value into a 64-bit value, and the recompiled C then differs from the original. A wrong field offset makes stage 3 miss the relocation on the `lea` that holds the jump table base.

The listing gives you an oracle with no judgment in it. You do not decide that your decode looks right. You compare it.

## The subset

| group | encodings |
|---|---|
| prefixes | `66`, `67`, `f2`, `f3`, `f0`, segment overrides `2e 36 3e 26 64 65`, then one REX byte `40` to `4f` |
| ALU | `01 09 11 19 21 29 31 39 85 89` (Ev, Gv), `03 0b 13 1b 23 2b 33 3b 8b` (Gv, Ev), accumulator forms, groups `81 83` |
| data | `88 8a`, `8d` lea, `b8`+r mov, `c7 /0`, `63` movslq, `0f b6 b7 be bf` movzx and movsx |
| arithmetic | `69 6b 0f af` imul, `c1 d1` shifts, `f7` test, not, neg, mul, imul, div, idiv, `99` cltd, `ff /0 /1` |
| control | `70`-`7f`, `0f 80`-`8f`, `e8`, `e9`, `eb`, `ff /2 /4`, `c3`, `0f 90`-`9f` setcc, `0f 40`-`4f` cmovcc |
| other | `90`, `0f 1f` multi-byte nop, `cc`, `0f 0b`, `50`-`5f` push and pop |

Anything else raises `DecodeError` with the address and the opcode bytes.

## Work through one concrete case

At address 0x3 of `tenths_and_fifths` at `-O1`, the bytes are `48 69 c0 67 66 66 66`.

| offset | byte | field | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `48` | REX | W=1, so the operand size is 64 bits |
| 1 | `69` | opcode | `imul Gv, Ev, Iz`: three operands, 32-bit immediate |
| 2 | `c0` | ModRM | mod=3 (register form), reg=0 (`rax`), rm=0 (`rax`) |
| 3 to 6 | `67 66 66 66` | immediate | 0x66666667, sign-extended to 64 bits |

The result is `imulq $0x66666667, %rax, %rax`, length 7, width 64, `immediate_offset` 3. Remove the `48` and the same bytes decode as `imull` with a 32-bit operand size. The two forms compute different values, and stage 5 recognizes the division idiom only in the 64-bit product.

A memory operand at `-O0`: `48 63 04 81` at 0x6f is `movslq (%rcx,%rax,4), %rax`. ModRM `04` has mod=0 and rm=4, so a SIB byte follows. SIB `81` has scale 1 << 2 = 4, index 0 (`rax`) and base 1 (`rcx`).

A RIP-relative operand: `48 8d 0d 00 00 00 00` at 0x5c is `leaq (%rip), %rcx`. ModRM `0d` has mod=0 and rm=5, which in 64-bit mode means RIP plus a 32-bit displacement. The displacement field starts at offset 3, so its absolute address is 0x5f. That is the `r_offset` of the relocation from stage 1.

A branch: `77 0c` at 0x58 is `ja` with an 8-bit displacement of 12. The target is the end of the instruction plus 12: 0x5a + 0xc = 0x66.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-2
```

Type other bytes into the lab, for example `48 63 04 81` or `66 0f 1f 44 00 00`, and read the field table before you write the decoder branch for them.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `decoder` module. The starter supplies the operand classes, the `Instruction` dataclass, the AT&T renderer, `_Cursor`, the `_State` helpers (`operand_size`, `register`, `immediate`, `displacement`, `finish`, `relative`), `parse_objdump`, `compare_with_objdump` and `disassemble`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `decode(code: bytes, address: int) -> Instruction` | `address` is an index into `code`. Read legacy prefixes, then at most one REX byte, then the opcode; `0f` selects the two-byte map. An address outside `code` raises `DecodeError`. |
| `_State.modrm(reg_width, rm_width) -> (Reg, Reg or Mem, int)` | Read ModRM, then SIB and displacement for memory forms. REX.R extends reg, REX.X the index, REX.B rm or the base. mod 0 with rm 5 is RIP-relative. SIB index 4 means no index; SIB base 5 with mod 0 means no base and a 32-bit displacement. |
| `_one_byte(state, opcode) -> Instruction` | The one-byte opcodes of the subset table. |
| `_two_byte(state, opcode) -> Instruction` | The `0f` opcodes of the subset table. |
| `linear_sweep(code, start=0, end=None) -> SweepResult` | Decode from `start` to `end`. On `DecodeError`, record `(address, byte)` in `undecodable` and continue at the next byte. |

Operand order follows AT&T: source first, destination last. `Instruction.flow` is `next`, `branch`, `jump`, `call`, `return`, `indirect-jump` or `indirect-call`. Immediates are signed, except for `mov` and shift counts, which the listing prints unsigned.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 2 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec disasm samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --oracle samples/samples-x86_64-O1.objdump.txt
```

The starter copied the fixture objects and listings into `samples`. You can also pass your own object and a listing you captured with `llvm-objdump -d -r`. The command prints every instruction with the relocation target after it, and then reports `oracle: 56/56 instructions agree with llvm-objdump`. The `-O0` object has 102 instructions. The held-out objects have 76 and 38.

## Failure cases

- `90 0f 0a` decoded at address 1 raises `DecodeError` whose reason names `0f 0a`.
- `48 69 c0 67 66` stops inside the immediate and raises instead of reading past the end.
- Fifteen `66` prefixes and a `90` is 16 bytes, which is longer than the 15-byte architectural limit, and raises.
- `31 c0 0f 0a c3` swept linearly gives `xorl %eax, %eax`, two undecodable bytes at 2 and 3, and `retq`.

## Extensions

- Add `movsd` and `cvtsi2sd` with the `f2` prefix and XMM registers, and extend the oracle check to a fixture that uses `double`.
- Add VEX prefixes (`c4`, `c5`) and decode one AVX instruction from your own compiled loop.
- Make `linear_sweep` restart at the next function symbol after a decode error, and measure how many instructions it recovers.

stages.title: Recover control flow
stages.summary: Follow control flow by recursive descent, resolve the position-independent jump table from its relocations and bounds check, split basic blocks, then compute dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. An indirect jump with no matching idiom stays unresolved and is reported.
stages.doc:
Stage 3 of 8. This stage applies [Disassembly and Control Flow](/learn/33-disassembly-and-control-flow), sections "Recursive Descent", "Basic Blocks", "Dominators With the Iterative Algorithm" and "The Jump Table in grade at -O0", and [Compiler Idioms and Optimization](/learn/39-compiler-idioms-and-optimization) for the bounds-check idiom.

## What you build

You build the control-flow graph of one function:

1. `recursive_descent` decodes only the bytes that control flow reaches from the entry.
2. A jump table resolver turns `jmpq *%rax` into a list of targets, with the table found through its relocation and its length taken from the bounds check.
3. `ControlFlowGraph` splits the instructions into basic blocks with typed edges: `jump`, `taken`, `fallthrough` and `table`.
4. The graph computes reverse postorder, immediate dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops.

## Why it matters

A linear sweep decodes alignment padding as if it were code. Recursive descent decodes only what can run, but it stops at an indirect jump unless something tells it where the jump goes. For the fixtures that something is the relocation on the `lea` that loads the table base and the relocations inside the table.

Dominators are the input of everything after this stage. SSA places phis on dominance frontiers (stage 4). A back edge is an edge to a block that dominates its source, and every loop that stage 7 emits starts from one. The immediate post-dominator of a branch is the place where its two arms join again, and stage 7 uses it to close an `if`.

## Work through one concrete case

`band` at `-O0` occupies 0x50 to 0xba, with 6 bytes of padding up to 0xc0.

Without a resolver, recursive descent from 0x50 decodes 16 instructions. It follows the `ja` at 0x62 to the default block at 0xae, falls through to 0x64, and stops at `jmpq *%rax` at 0x76. That jump is listed in `unresolved`, and the six case blocks are never reached.

The resolver walks back from the jump:

| address | instruction | role |
|---|---|---|
| 0x5e | `subq $0x5, %rax` | bounds check against 5 |
| 0x62 | `ja 0xae` | out of range goes to default |
| 0x68 | `leaq (%rip), %rcx` | table base, relocation `.rodata-0x4` resolves to `.rodata+0x0` |
| 0x6f | `movslq (%rcx,%rax,4), %rax` | load a 4-byte signed entry |
| 0x73 | `addq %rcx, %rax` | entry plus base |
| 0x76 | `jmpq *%rax` | the indirect jump |

The bounds check allows indexes 0 to 5, so the table has 6 entries. Each entry has a `.rodata` relocation against `.text`. Entry i is at `.rodata+4i`, so its target is `addend + (table base - entry offset)`: 0x78, 0x81, 0x8a, 0x93, 0x9c and 0xa5. With the resolver the descent decodes 28 instructions, and the linear sweep of the same range decodes 29 because it also decodes the `nopw` padding.

The graph has 10 blocks and 15 edges, six of them `table` edges. The immediate dominator of every case block is 0x64, the block that holds the jump. The default block 0xae and the return block 0xb5 have immediate dominator 0x50, because both the default path and the case paths reach them. The immediate post-dominator of the entry is 0xb5.

At `-O1` the same `switch` has no indirect jump. clang loaded the result from a value table with `movl (%rcx,%rax,4), %eax`. `find_value_tables` reports that table, reads its six 4-byte values from the bytes (5, 8, 12, 20, 20, 35), and marks the evidence as `bytes`, because no relocation is inside a value table.

`fold` at `-O1` is a rotated loop. Its blocks start at 0x70, 0x74, 0x80, 0x92 and 0x93. The block at 0x80 branches back to itself, so (0x80, 0x80) is the only back edge, the natural loop is `{0x80}`, and the dominance frontier of 0x80 is `{0x80}`. At `-O0` the loop has its exit test in the header: the back edge is 0xe1 to 0xd9, and the post-dominator of the header is the exit block 0xfe.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-3
```

Add the back edge to the entry in the lab. The entry has no predecessor inside the function but has an implicit edge from the caller, so the entry enters its own dominance frontier. The `dominance_frontiers` contract below requires that case.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `cfg` module. The starter supplies `JumpTable`, `Descent`, `Block`, `FunctionGraph`, `find_value_tables`, `build_cfg`, `dominates`, `ControlFlowGraph.dominators`, `summary` and the register helpers.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `recursive_descent(code, entries, end=None, resolver=None) -> Descent` | Worklist from `entries`. A jump continues at its target, a branch at both successors, a call after itself, a return stops. An address inside a decoded instruction is a conflict `(address, instruction start)`. An undecodable byte stops that path and is listed. An indirect jump stops unless `resolver` returns a `JumpTable`. An entry outside `[0, end)` raises `ValueError`. |
| `bounds_check(instructions, before) -> (limit, address)` | The last `cmp $N` or `sub $N` followed by `ja` before `before`. Returns `(None, None)` when there is none. |
| `recover_table(elf, instructions, load, jump, section=".text") -> JumpTable or None` | Find the RIP-relative `lea` that wrote the base register of `load`, resolve its relocation, take `limit + 1` entries of `scale` bytes, from relocations when present and from bytes otherwise. |
| `jump_table_resolver(elf, section=".text") -> Resolver` | Match `lea table(%rip), base; movslq (base, index, 4), reg; add base, reg; jmp *reg` backwards from the jump. |
| `ControlFlowGraph(entry, instructions, tables=None)` | `_leaders`, then `_build`: blocks with typed successor edges. The entry must be a decoded address or `ValueError` is raised. |
| `reverse_postorder()`, `back_edges()`, `natural_loops()`, `post_dominators()` | As named. Post-dominators use a virtual `EXIT` node that every return block reaches. |
| `immediate_dominators(entry, order, predecessors) -> dict` | The iterative algorithm of Cooper, Harvey and Kennedy over reverse postorder. |
| `dominance_frontiers(idom, predecessors) -> dict[int, set[int]]` | For a join with two or more predecessors, walk each predecessor up the dominator tree to the join's immediate dominator. For the entry, a predecessor walk continues up to and including the entry. |

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 3 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec cfg samples/samples-x86_64-O0.o band
```

The JSON shows `unresolvedWithoutTables: ["0x76"]`, the table with `"evidence": "relocation"`, 10 blocks and the immediate dominator of each block.

## Failure cases

- An entry at 4 in a 1-byte range raises `ValueError`.
- `74 03 b8 01 00 00 00 c3`: the `je` targets 5, which is inside the `mov` at 2. The descent records the conflict `(5, 2)` and keeps the instructions at 0, 2 and 7.
- `31 c0 0f 0a c3`: the path stops at the undecodable byte at 2, which is listed as unresolved.
- `48 8b 45 f0 ff e0 c3`: an indirect jump through a value loaded from the stack matches no idiom. It stays unresolved, and the graph summary lists `0x4`.

## Extensions

- Resolve the absolute jump table form `jmpq *table(,%rax,8)` that non-PIC code uses, with `R_X86_64_32S` relocations.
- Detect a tail call: a `jmp` to another function symbol. Treat it as a call followed by a return.
- Compute the loop nesting forest for irreducible graphs and report the extra entries of each loop.

stages.title: Lift to IR and build SSA
stages.summary: Lift each instruction to a small IR in which flags are an ordinary variable, frame bookkeeping disappears and frame-pointer slots become locals. Place phi statements on iterated dominance frontiers and rename over the dominator tree so every value has one definition, with explicit casts where a narrow definition meets a wide use.
stages.doc:
Stage 4 of 8. This stage applies [Lifting to Pseudocode](/learn/34-lifting-to-pseudocode), sections "Stage 3: Lifting to a Small IR" and "Stage 5: SSA, One Name per Definition", and [Calling Conventions and Stack Frames](/learn/38-calling-conventions-and-stack-frames) for the frame-pointer prologue.

## What you build

You build two things.

The lifter turns each decoded instruction into IR statements. The IR has assignments, stores, branches, jumps, a switch through a recovered table and returns. Its expressions are constants, variables with a width, binary operations, casts, loads, flag records and section addresses. Registers become variables named by their 64-bit family (`eax` writes `rax` at width 32). The flags register is an ordinary variable named `flags`. Frame bookkeeping (`push`, `pop`, `mov %rsp, %rbp`, stack adjustments) produces no statements, and a slot at a constant offset from `%rbp` becomes a local variable such as `local_8`.

The SSA builder gives every definition its own version. It places phi statements on the iterated dominance frontier of each variable's definition sites, renames uses over the dominator tree, and inserts a cast where a use has a different width than the definition it reads.

## Why it matters

x86-64 instructions do several things at once. `subl %edi, %esi` writes `%esi` and six flags. A later `jle` reads two of those flags. If the lifter writes the flags as a variable, stage 5 can see that `jle` after `testl %esi, %esi` means `esi <= 0`, and dead code removal can delete every flag write that no branch reads.

SSA makes every later question local. "Which value does this use read?" has one answer, the single definition with that version. A value that arrives from two paths is a phi, and the phi lists which predecessor provides which version.

## Work through one concrete case

`fold` at `-O1` has five blocks. Before SSA, the lifted loop block 0x80 reads:

```text
block 0x80 -> 0x80, 0x92
  eax = eax << 5
  flags = cmp(eax, esi)
  eax = eax - esi
  flags = add(eax, load32(rdi + rdx * 4))
  eax = eax + load32(rdi + rdx * 4)
  flags = inc(rdx, 1)
  rdx = rdx + 1
  esi = eax
  flags = cmp(rcx, rdx)
  if jne(flags) goto 0x80 else goto 0x92
```

The variables defined inside the loop are `eax`, `rdx`, `esi` and `flags`. The loop header 0x80 is in its own dominance frontier, because the back edge comes from 0x80 itself. So `insert_phis` places four phis at 0x80, one per variable. `ecx` is defined only in 0x74, whose frontier is empty, so it gets no phi.

Renaming walks the dominator tree 0x70, 0x74, 0x80, then 0x92 and 0x93:

```text
block 0x74 -> 0x80
  ecx_1 = esi_0
  edx_1 = 0
  esi_1 = 0
  eax_1 = esi_1
block 0x80 -> 0x80, 0x92
  esi_2 = phi(0x74: esi_1, 0x80: esi_3)
  rdx_2 = phi(0x74: edx_1, 0x80: rdx_3)
  eax_2 = phi(0x74: eax_1, 0x80: eax_5)
  flags_2 = phi(0x74: flags_1, 0x80: flags_6)
  ...
  flags_6 = cmp(zext64(ecx_1), rdx_3)
```

Version 0 is the value at function entry: `esi_0` is the second argument and `rdi_0` the first. Two width facts appear here. `ecx_1` is a 32-bit definition and `cmp(rcx, rdx)` reads 64 bits, so the use becomes `zext64(ecx_1)`; writing a 32-bit register clears the upper half. The `rdx` phi has a 32-bit source (`edx_1 = 0`) and a 64-bit source (`rdx_3`), so the phi is widened to 64 bits.

At `-O0` the same loop keeps its values in stack slots. `movl %edi, -0x8(%rbp)` lifts to `local_8 = rdi`, and the loop header 0xd9 gets phis for `local_10` and `local_14`.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-4
```

Move the definitions of `x` between blocks in the lab. A definition in only one arm puts a phi at the join. With the back edge to the entry, the entry gets a phi whose first source is the entry value `x_0`.

## Implement the contract

Implement these. The starter supplies the IR dataclasses, `LiftContext`, `children`, `rebuild`, `rewrite`, `iter_nodes`, `variables`, `stmt_exprs`, `map_stmt`, `IrPrinter` and `to_ssa`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `lift_instruction(insn, ctx) -> list` | One instruction to IR statements. `sub` and `cmp` write `Flags("cmp", destination, source)`; `test` writes `Flags("test", ...)`; `xor r, r` and `sub r, r` write constant 0. `cltd` writes `rdx = signfill(rax)`; `idivl` writes `dividend = rdx:rax`, then the quotient and remainder. A RIP-relative operand with a relocation is a `Symbolic(section, offset)`. A call becomes `rax = call name(args)` using known signatures. An instruction with no rule raises `LiftError` with its address. Signedness evidence goes into `ctx.signedness`. |
| `lift_function(elf, graph, signatures=None) -> Function` | Lift every reachable block in address order. Unreachable blocks and unresolved jumps go into `notes`. Copy the dominators from the graph into `fn.idom`. |
| `insert_phis(fn) -> int` | Phis on the iterated dominance frontier of every variable's definition sites. A phi at the entry block also takes `Var(name, 0, 0)` keyed by `EXIT`. Returns the number placed. |
| `rename(fn)` | One version stack per variable over the dominator tree; version 0 is the entry value. Record every definition width in `fn.def_width`, widen each phi to its widest source, and wrap each use whose width differs from its definition in `zext` or `trunc`. |
| `check_single_assignment(fn) -> list[str]` | The `name_version` keys defined more than once. An empty list means the function is in SSA form. |

IR statements are mutable and compared by identity. Expressions are frozen and compared by value.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 4 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec decompile samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --function fold --ir
```

The `--ir` output prints the IR before SSA and the SSA form. The decompiled C at the end of the output needs stages 5 to 7.

## Failure cases

- `cmovg` (`0f 4f c1`) decodes, but the lifter has no rule for it and raises `LiftError` naming 0x40.
- A use of a register before any write is version 0, and stage 6 decides whether it is an argument.
- A phi that receives a 32-bit and a 64-bit version is widened; leaving it at 32 bits would truncate the loop index in the emitted C.
- A loop whose header is the entry needs the entry value as a phi source. Without it, the first iteration reads an undefined version.

## Extensions

- Lift `setcc` and `cmovcc` to conditional expressions and test them on a fixture with a ternary operator.
- Split the flags variable into the six individual flags and show which branches read only ZF.
- Replace the minimal phi placement with pruned SSA: skip a phi when the variable is not live at the join.

stages.title: Simplify and fold idioms
stages.summary: Turn flag conditions into comparisons, propagate copies and constants, delete dead definitions, merge congruent phis and substitute single-use values without moving a load across a store. Recognize the multiply-and-shift form of signed division by a constant and fold it only when the multiplier, shift and error bound prove the divisor.
stages.doc:
Stage 5 of 8. This stage applies [Lifting to Pseudocode](/learn/34-lifting-to-pseudocode), section "Stage 6: Simplify, Substitute, Remove Dead Code", and [Compiler Idioms and Optimization](/learn/39-compiler-idioms-and-optimization) for division by a constant.

## What you build

You build the passes that turn SSA statements into expressions a person can read:

- a bottom-up simplifier that turns a branch on flags into a comparison, folds constants, removes `+ 0` and `* 1`, folds nested casts, turns a scaled load into an element access `base[index]` and an offset load into a field access `base->field_4`,
- copy and constant propagation,
- dead code elimination,
- merging of phis that carry the same value on every edge,
- single-use substitution that never moves a load across a store or a call,
- recognition of signed division by a constant.

`optimize` repeats them until no pass changes anything.

## Why it matters

After stage 4, `tenths_and_fifths` at `-O1` is 14 statements of multiplies, shifts and flag writes. Its source is one line. The passes in this stage recover that line, and each step can be checked: a pass that changes the value of the function makes the stage 8 differential test fail.

The division idiom is the case where a wrong fold is easy to write. A multiplier that is close to the right one gives the correct quotient for small inputs and a wrong one for large inputs. The fold is allowed only when the arithmetic proves it.

## Work through one concrete case

At `-O1`, clang compiled `value / 10 + value / 5` as:

```text
movslq  %edi, %rax
imulq   $0x66666667, %rax, %rax
movq    %rax, %rcx
sarq    $0x22, %rcx        shift 34
movq    %rax, %rdx
shrq    $0x3f, %rdx        sign bit of the product
addl    %edx, %ecx         quotient for 10
sarq    $0x21, %rax        shift 33
addl    %edx, %eax         quotient for 5
addl    %ecx, %eax
```

The form is `((long)x * m >> s) + sign bit`. To recover the divisor, `magic_divisor(m, s)` tries d = floor(2^s / m) and d + 1, and keeps the d for which m is the ceiling of 2^s / d and the error stays small (Granlund and Montgomery, 1994):

| m | s | d | m * d - 2^s | bound 2^s / 2^31 | fold |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0x66666667 | 34 | 10 | 6 | 8 | yes |
| 0x66666667 | 33 | 5 | 3 | 4 | yes |
| 0x55555556 | 32 | 3 | 2 | 2 | yes |
| 0x66666668 | 34 | none | | | no |

Check one input by hand. For x = -7 and d = 10, the product is -7 * 1717986919 = -12025908433. Shifting right by 34 rounds toward minus infinity and gives -1. The sign bit of the product is 1. The sum is 0, which equals the C result of -7 / 10. `division_identity_holds` repeats this check on a sample that includes `INT_MIN`, `INT_MAX` and the values from -40 to 40 before the pass folds.

After SSA the two shared values are `rax_2 = rax_1 * 0x66666667` and `rdx_2 = rax_2 >>u 63`. The simplifier finds `trunc32(rcx_2) + trunc32(rdx_2)` where `rcx_2 = rax_2 >>s 34`, follows both sides to the same product, and replaces the sum with `edi_0 / 10`. Dead code removal then deletes the product, the shifts and every flag write, because nothing reads them. The function ends as one statement:

```text
return edi_0 / 10 + edi_0 / 5
```

`thirds` uses `shrq $0x20` for the quotient. The result is truncated to 32 bits, and for a shift of exactly 32 the low 32 bits of a logical shift equal those of an arithmetic shift. So the pass accepts a logical shift only when the shift is 32.

For `fold`, the loop condition `flags_6 = cmp(zext64(ecx_1), rdx_3)` with `jne` becomes `zext64(esi_0) != rdx_3` after copy propagation replaces `ecx_1` with `esi_0`. Two of the four loop phis carry the same value on every edge (`eax_2` and `esi_2`), so one is merged into the other and two phis remain.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-5
```

Set the divisor to 10 and the shift to 33 in the lab. The multiplier is 0x33333334 and the error is 8, which is twice the bound of 4, so the pass must leave the multiply in the output.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `passes` module. The starter supplies `c_div`, `truncate`, `OptimizeReport`, `place_of`, `definition_order`, `count_uses`, `has_call`, `contains_load`, `stmt_has_side_effect` and `simplify_function`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `magic_divisor(multiplier, shift) -> int or None` | The divisor d > 1 such that the multiplier is ceil(2^shift / d) and `multiplier * d - 2^shift <= 2^shift >> 31`. `None` for a shift outside 32 to 63 or a multiplier that is not positive. |
| `division_identity_holds(multiplier, shift, divisor, samples=None) -> bool` | Evaluate the idiom with 64-bit wraparound on every sample and compare with `c_div`. |
| `make_simplifier(defs, recognize_division, report=None, order=None)` | Return a function for `rewrite` that applies the rules listed in "What you build". Record each folded division in `report.divisions` once. |
| `remove_dead_code(fn, uses) -> int` | Delete an assignment or phi whose destination has no use, except an assignment that contains a call. |
| `propagate_copies(fn) -> int` | Replace uses of `x = y` (same width) and `x = constant`, but never inside a phi source. |
| `substitute_once(fn, uses) -> bool` | Move one single-use definition into its use in the same block. A value that contains a load does not move across a store or a call. |
| `merge_congruent_phis(fn) -> int` | Two phis in one block with equal values on every edge and the same width: replace the later with the earlier. |
| `optimize(fn, recognize_division=True, rounds=400) -> OptimizeReport` | Simplify, then run dead code, copies, phi merging and substitution in that order, restarting after any change. |

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 5 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec decompile samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --function tenths_and_fifths --ir
python3 -m minidec decompile samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --function tenths_and_fifths --ir --no-division-idioms
```

The first command prints `return edi_0 / 10 + edi_0 / 5` in the optimized IR. The second keeps `0x66666667`, `>>s 34` and `>>u 63`.

## Failure cases

- `magic_divisor(0x66666667, 31)` is `None`: a shift below 32 cannot come from this idiom.
- `magic_divisor(0x66666668, 34)` is `None`: one more than the right multiplier fails the ceiling check.
- `division_identity_holds(0x66666667, 34, 11)` is false.
- In `record`, the load of `m->reads` comes before the store to `m->reads`. Substitution must keep `ecx_2 = rdi_0->field_0 + 1` above `store32(rdi_0) = ecx_2`, or the C reads the new value.

## Extensions

- Recognize unsigned division, which uses `mul` and `shr` with no sign correction, and the forms clang emits when the multiplier does not fit in 32 bits.
- Recognize `x % d` as `x - (x / d) * d` after the division fold.
- Add global value numbering and compare the statement count of every fixture function before and after.

stages.title: Recover the signature and types
stages.summary: A System V argument register read before any write is a parameter, and the highest one fixes the count. Coalesce phi webs into C variables, make a scaled element access a pointer to its element and constant offsets a struct, and choose signedness from the instructions that touch each value. Every choice carries its instruction evidence.
stages.doc:
Stage 6 of 8. This stage applies [Calling Conventions and Stack Frames](/learn/38-calling-conventions-and-stack-frames), section "System V: Two Independent Register Sequences and a Red Zone", [Lifting to Pseudocode](/learn/34-lifting-to-pseudocode), sections "Stage 4: Parameters From the Calling Convention" and "Stage 7: Types From Use", and [Recovering Data and Types](/learn/41-recovering-data-and-types).

## What you build

You build signature recovery for the optimized SSA function:

1. **Parameters.** The System V psABI passes the first six INTEGER arguments in `%rdi`, `%rsi`, `%rdx`, `%rcx`, `%r8` and `%r9`. A register read at version 0 is read before any write. The highest such argument register fixes the count, so a function that reads only `%rsi` still has two parameters. A read of another register before any write is an undefined read. The recovery reports it and does not make it a parameter.
2. **Webs.** A phi and its sources are one C variable. Union-find joins them, and each web gets one name: `param_N` for an argument, `local_8` for a stack slot, `eax_1` for a register value.
3. **Types.** The widest definition in a web gives `int` or `long`. A web used as the base of a scaled element access becomes a pointer to the element. A web used as the base of constant offsets becomes a pointer to a struct with one field per offset. Pointer types spread along copies and phis.
4. **Signedness.** Arithmetic shifts, signed division, signed compares and sign extension say signed. Logical shifts and unsigned division say unsigned. A lone unsigned compare is the range-check idiom of a `switch`, and it does not make the value unsigned.
5. **Return type.** The width of the value in `%rax` at each return. If no path writes `%rax`, the result is `void`, and that guess is listed as an unknown.

Every decision carries the instructions that support it.

## Why it matters

The machine code has no types. A wrong parameter count changes the call in the stage 8 driver. A wrong width truncates a `long`. A wrong signedness flips the result of a compare for negative inputs. Each of these produces C that compiles and computes the wrong answer, so each type has to point at its evidence.

## Work through one concrete case

`record` at `-O1` after stage 5:

```text
block 0xa0 -> exit
  ecx_2 = rdi_0->field_0 + 1
  store32(rdi_0) = ecx_2
  eax_2 = esi_0 + rdi_0->field_4
  store32(rdi_0 + 4) = eax_2
  return eax_2 / ecx_2
```

Version 0 reads: `rdi_0` and `esi_0`. The highest argument register is `%rsi`, so there are two parameters. `rdi` is read at 64 bits and `esi` at 32 bits.

`rdi_0` is the base of `field_0` and `field_4`, both 32 bits wide. The web of `rdi_0` becomes `struct record_param_1 *` with fields at 0x0 and 0x4. The return value is 32 bits wide. The signature report:

```json
{
  "declaration": "int record(struct record_param_1 *param_1, int param_2)",
  "params": [
    {"name": "param_1", "register": "rdi", "width": 64, "ctype": "struct record_param_1 *", "signedness": "pointer",
     "evidence": ["%rdi is read before any write", "accessed through constant offsets 0x0, 0x4"]},
    {"name": "param_2", "register": "rsi", "width": 32, "ctype": "int", "signedness": "none",
     "evidence": ["%esi is read before any write"]}
  ],
  "structs": {"record_param_1": {"0x0": 32, "0x4": 32}},
  "evidence": ["2 argument register(s) read before write", "return value width 32 from the value in %rax at every return",
               "signed instructions: 0xae cltd; 0xaf idivl %ecx"]
}
```

`param_2` has signedness `none`: no instruction touches it directly with a signed or unsigned choice, so `int` is a default and stage 7 lists that as an unknown.

Three more fixture results:

| function | declaration | deciding evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `fold` | `int fold(int *param_1, int param_2)` | `(rdi, rdx, 4)` is a scaled 4-byte access; `jle` on `param_2` is signed |
| `band` | `int band(int param_1)` | only `cmp $5` and `ja` touch it: `unsigned-compare`, the range check |
| `tenths_and_fifths` without the division fold | `int tenths_and_fifths(int param_1)` | `movslq` and `sarq` say signed |

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-6
```

Clear `%rdi` but keep `%rsi` in the lab. The count stays at two, because the psABI assigns registers by position. Change the `%esi` evidence to `cmp then ja`: the type stays `int` and the signedness becomes `unsigned-compare`.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `types` module. The starter supplies `Param`, `Signature`, `ctype`, `utype`, `declaration` and `live_keys`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `collect_params(fn)` | Set `fn.params` to the argument registers up to the highest one read at version 0, `fn.param_widths` from `fn.def_width`, and `fn.undefined_reads` to other version 0 reads except `flags` and `rax`. |
| `coalesce_webs(fn)` | Union every phi with its sources. Set `fn.web_names` for every SSA key and `fn.web_types` to `int` or `long` from the widest member. |
| `signedness_by_web(fn) -> dict[str, set[str]]` | For each web label, the evidence kinds: `signed`, `unsigned-arithmetic`, `unsigned-compare`. |
| `signedness_label(kinds) -> str` | `none`, `signed`, `unsigned`, `unsigned-compare` or `mixed`. `signed` with anything else is `mixed`; any `unsigned-arithmetic` without `signed` is `unsigned`. |
| `infer_types(fn)` | Element pointers, struct pointers with `fn.structs`, unsigned types for `unsigned` webs, and `fn.return_type`. |
| `recover_signature(fn) -> Signature` | Run the four steps above and build the `Signature` with parameter evidence and instruction evidence. |

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --stage 6 --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec decompile samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --function record --json
```

The `--json` output carries the signature report with its evidence. The C text above it needs stage 7.

## Failure cases

- A function that reads only `%esi` has two parameters, and `param_1` is unused.
- A function that reads `%r10` before writing it has no parameter for it. `r10` goes into `undefinedReads`, and its web is named `undefined_r10`.
- A function that returns without writing `%rax` is `void`, with an unknown that says a caller could contradict it.
- A value that both `sarl` and `shrl` touch is `mixed`. The type stays signed, and the unsigned use gets a cast in stage 7.

## Extensions

- Read stack arguments above the return address for a seventh parameter, and floating-point arguments from `%xmm0` to `%xmm7`.
- Merge the struct layouts of two functions that receive the same pointer, and report conflicting widths at one offset.
- Detect a returned struct passed in `%rax` and `%rdx`, and a large struct returned through a hidden pointer in `%rdi`.

stages.title: Structure the graph and emit C
stages.summary: Match loops, two-way and n-way conditionals with the immediate post-dominator as the join, emit if, if-else, while, do-while and switch, and print C with recovered struct and table definitions. A region that matches no shape produces a counted goto, and every heuristic goes into the unknowns list.

stages.title: Prove the output
stages.summary: Recompile the emitted C with the fixture flags, compare each function with relocation fields masked, compare the constants each relocation points at, and run original and candidate side by side over an input grid that crosses limits, zero, negatives and compare constants. The report is fail-closed and lists every unknown. Without clang the recompile and differential legs skip and say why.
stages.doc:
Stage 8 of 8. This stage applies [Rebuild and Prove Equal](/learn/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal), sections "Leg One: Execute and Compare" and "Leg Two: Recompile and Compare", and [Evidence, Confidence, and Unknowns in Binary Analysis](/learn/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns) for the report.

## What you build

You build `verify`, the command that turns decompiled text into a claim with evidence. It has two legs and one report.

**Bytes leg.** Recompile `decompiled.c` with the fixture flags (`-target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -O1 -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -c`). For each function, cut the original and the candidate out of their objects, zero every relocation field in both, and compare. Then compare the relocation records by offset, type and target section, and compare the words that each PC-relative relocation points at in a data section. Equal masked bytes with different table contents is a difference.

**Behaviour leg.** Compile the original source, the candidate with every function renamed to `cand_<name>`, and a generated C driver. Feed the driver one line per input cell. It calls both versions on copies of the same memory, prints both results and the memory after the call, and prints `trap` when a division traps. Any cell where the two lines differ is a mismatch.

**Report.** `report.json` lists, per function, the signature, the behaviour status with cell counts by kind, the bytes status with reasons, and every unknown from stage 7 plus every leg that did not run. The aggregate is fail-closed.

## Why it matters

Readable C proves nothing. A decompiler output that looks right can swap a signed compare for an unsigned one and still compile. The behaviour leg runs it. A decompiler output that runs right on a few inputs can still differ for `INT_MIN`. The grid crosses the limits on purpose. The bytes leg asks a stricter question: does the same compiler with the same flags produce the same function? When the answer is yes, the C is a source for that function at that optimization level.

## The input grid

Each parameter gets a value set, and the sets are crossed, capped at 400 cells:

| parameter | values |
|---|---|
| int, no pointer parameter in the function | 0, 1, -1, 2, 7, 10, -10, 100, `INT_MAX`, `INT_MIN` |
| int, beside a pointer | 0, 1, 3, 8, -1, 100 (the count stays inside the 4096-word buffer) |
| every compare constant c | c - 1, c and c + 1 are added |
| pointer | five 8-word patterns: zeros, ascending, mixed signs, limits, all -1 |

Each cell is labelled `limit`, `compare-edge`, `zero`, `negative` or `plain` so the report shows what the grid covered.

## Work through one concrete case

Run the command on the committed `-O1` object and its source:

```bash
python3 -m minidec verify samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --source samples/samples.c --opt O1 --out verify-O1
```

| function | cells | behaviour | bytes | reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tenths_and_fifths` | 10 | pass | pass | |
| `thirds` | 100 | pass | pass | |
| `band` | 13 | pass | pass | |
| `fold` | 30 | pass | differs | size 38 vs 40 bytes |
| `record` | 30 | pass | pass | |

`band` has 13 cells: the 10 base values plus 4, 5 and 6 from its compare constant 5. Those three cells are `compare-edge`. Its masked bytes are equal, and its relocation points at `.rodata+0x0` in both objects, where both hold `[5, 8, 12, 20, 20, 35]`.

`fold` passes all 30 behaviour cells, but the recompiled loop is 2 bytes longer. The decompiled loop compares a `long` counter with a zero-extended count, where the source uses an `int` index, and clang emits a different instruction sequence for that loop. The aggregate is `behaviour-only`: the program computes the same values on the grid, and the bytes are not the same.

The masking step on `band` at `-O1`: the function is 0x17 bytes, its one relocation is at offset 0xf with width 4, so bytes 0xf to 0x12 become zero in both copies before the compare.

A candidate made from the same source with one table value changed (case 4 returns 21) has equal masked bytes and equal relocation shapes. Only the constant check sees `[5, 8, 12, 20, 21, 35]`, so its status is `differs` with the reason "referenced constants differ".

At `-O0` the aggregate is also `behaviour-only`: `band` differs in size (106 vs 114 bytes); its emitted switch uses a `long` index variable that the source does not have. `record` differs in 8 bytes; the emitted C keeps no stack copies of the parameters, and the `-O0` original does.

```figure
pj-mini-decompiler-8
```

Add a pointer parameter in the lab and watch the per-scalar values drop from 10 to 6 and the cell count multiply by 5. Clear the `clang on PATH` box: both legs become `unknown`, and so does the aggregate.

## Implement the contract

Implement these in the `verify` module. The starter supplies the constants, `fixture_flags`, `find_clang`, `host_description`, `read_referenced`, `ByteComparison`, `Cell`, `driver_source`, `Harness`, `build_harness`, `parse_result`, `run_cells` and `BehaviourReport`.

| function | contract |
|---|---|
| `recompile(source, opt, out) -> Path` | Run clang with `fixture_flags(opt)`. Missing clang or a compile error raises `VerifyError` with the compiler text. |
| `mask_relocations(data, relocations) -> (bytes, ranges)` | Zero `width` bytes at each relocation offset; return the masked bytes and the `(offset, width)` ranges. |
| `compare_function_bytes(original, candidate, name, tables=None) -> ByteComparison` | Masked compare, relocation shape compare, referenced constant compare. A function missing from the candidate is `unknown`, never a pass. |
| `classify(args, constants) -> str` | The cell label, in the priority order of the grid section. |
| `input_grid(signature, constants=None, limit=400) -> list[Cell]` | The crossed value sets above, with no duplicate cells. |
| `differential_test(original_source, candidate_source, decompiled, opt, workdir)` | Build the harness and run every function's grid. |
| `aggregate(behaviour, bytes_status) -> str` | `fail` if any behaviour fails; `unknown` if there is no function or any leg is unknown; `pass` if all bytes pass; otherwise `behaviour-only`. |
| `evidence_report(...) -> dict` | The JSON report with the limits of each claim. |
| `verify(object_path, source_path=None, opt="O1", out_dir=None, functions=None, recognize_division=True) -> dict` | Decompile, write `decompiled.c`, recompile and compare bytes, run the grid when the source and clang exist, write `report.json`. |

The CLI `verify` command exits 0 for `pass` and `behaviour-only` and 1 for `fail` and `unknown`, so a CI job can gate on it.

## Verify and inspect

```bash
python3 scripts/project_test.py mini-decompiler --all --path learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler --strict
cd learning-artifacts/mini-decompiler
python3 -m minidec verify samples/samples-x86_64-O1.o --source samples/samples.c --opt O1 --out verify-O1
python3 -m minidec verify your-object.o --source your-source.c --opt O1 --out verify-yours
```

Without clang on `PATH`, the recompile and differential tests skip with the reason "clang is not on PATH: the recompile leg cannot run; the committed-object legs still ran". A skipped test prevents completion evidence, so install clang to finish the project. The masking, grid, driver, aggregate and committed-object tests run on every host.

## Failure cases

- `int f(int a) { return a +; }` makes `recompile` raise `VerifyError` that starts with "recompile failed".
- A candidate where `fold` uses a `long` accumulator is 45 bytes against 38, and the reason says "size 38 vs 45 bytes".
- Comparing `band` against an object that has no `band` is `unknown` with the function name in the reason.
- `verify` with no source writes behaviour `unknown` for every function, "was not compared" in the unknowns, and an aggregate of `unknown` even when every byte compare passes.
- `fixture_flags("O9")` raises `ValueError`.

## Limits of the claim

The behaviour leg compiles the original source and the candidate for the host. On an arm64 host it compares the behaviour of the C source, and it does not execute the committed x86-64 object. A pass covers the grid on this host and is not a proof of equivalence for every input. The bytes leg is a statement about one compiler version with one set of flags. Pointer parameters reach the driver as `void *`, which is correct for the psABI because the psABI passes every pointer in an INTEGER register.

## Extensions

- Run the committed x86-64 object itself under an x86-64 emulator so the behaviour leg also covers the original machine code.
- Add a random leg seeded from the object hash, and record the seed in the report so a mismatch can be replayed.
- Write a minimizer that shrinks a mismatching cell to the smallest input that still differs.
